sub_sections.title: Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development
sub_sections.content:
## 2.1 Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development

### The transformation FIELDWISE is designed to deliver

FIELDWISE is built around a deliberate and explicitly staged transformation of the researcher's professional profile. The experienced researcher enters the fellowship with a consolidated foundation in agronomy, plant protection and plant physiology and with developing expertise in Earth observation (EO), geographic information systems (GIS) and agricultural data science. The action is designed to close a specific and named competence gap — Bayesian and probabilistic modelling, spatio-temporal artificial intelligence, sensor-domain transfer, uncertainty quantification, domain adaptation and operational decision evaluation — so that the researcher exits able to take an agricultural-intelligence concept through the full arc from experimental evidence to a validated model, cross-country testing, commercial-field testing and a deployed web minimum viable product (MVP). This is precisely the increase in research and transferable skills that the call sets as its first expected outcome for supported fellows (EO-01, 'increased set of research and transferable skills and competences ... leading to improved employability and career prospects within academia and beyond') and that underpins the expected impact of improved researcher employability and career mobility within and beyond academia (EI-01). The intended progression is concrete: Plant Physiologist/Agronomist to EO/Geospatial Crop Scientist to Independent researcher in transferable agricultural intelligence. Every measure below is chosen because it moves the researcher along that trajectory and is evidenced by an activity the project actually carries out, not asserted in the abstract.

### Specific measures inside academia

**The Career Development Plan as the operational instrument.** The central, structuring measure is the Career Development Plan, formalised as an early project deliverable (D1.3 Career Development Plan, due M3, owned by the fellow and the supervisor). It is established jointly by both supervisors and the researcher and is signed by both supervisors and the fellow, which is how the joint-establishment requirement of the call (SR-05) is met once a co-supervisor is in place. The plan is not a one-off document: it is agreed by M3 and then reviewed at five steering points (M6, M12, M16, M20 and M27), so that training, career needs and progression are re-examined against evidence throughout the action and, critically, once more during the non-academic placement, which is when inter-sectoral career development is most in play. The plan carries six components — research objectives (O1 to O6); training and career needs; transferable skills; teaching; publications planning; and Open Science engagement — giving the evaluator a single, reviewable spine through which every career and skills measure is tracked. A dedicated key performance indicator (the Career Development Plan agreed by M3 and reviewed at all five steering points, tracing to D1.3) makes delivery and review of the plan measurable rather than declarative.

**Structured research-skills development through supervised practice and named courses.** The specific competences the researcher will acquire are delivered as supervised practice plus named ELTE courses across eleven host-to-fellow competence areas: geoinformatics; EO time-series analysis; optical/SAR integration; hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer; spatio-temporal modelling; Bayesian hierarchical modelling; uncertainty quantification; transfer learning and domain adaptation; reproducible geospatial computation; research software and web deployment; and intellectual property (IP) and research exploitation. These map directly onto the named competence gap and onto the work packages in which they are exercised, so the skills are learned by doing project science rather than in isolation. Supervision is intensive and structured to support this: a weekly one-to-one meeting with the supervisor, a weekly technical session with the co-supervisor through the core modelling and transferability phase (tapering to monthly thereafter), a monthly written progress record held by the fellow, and a quarterly review against the Career Development Plan attended by both supervisors. The co-supervisor provides the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development and testing, giving the researcher a dedicated route to advanced machine-learning and meta-modelling competence while she designs, builds and runs the models herself.

**Transferable and digital skills.** Seven transferable-skill strands are embedded in the plan: research integrity; Open Science and FAIR practice; generative-AI literacy; grant writing; IP and exploitation; project management; and science communication. This is a direct and complete answer to the call's training requirement (SR-04) that training activities integrate key transferable skills and competences — including digital skills such as generative AI — foster an Open Science culture and knowledge valorisation, and embed good scientific conduct including research integrity. Open Science is operationalised across the project ('as open as possible, as closed as necessary'), with expected open outputs including harmonisation protocols, validation split manifests, the hyperspectral-to-Sentinel methodology, analysis and model code where IP permits, model cards, FAIR metadata and open-access publications — so the Open-Science skill strand is practised on real project outputs.

**Teaching and academic-track development.** The teaching component is framed honestly as an existing strength transferred into a new context rather than a competence to be acquired: the researcher taught for five years at a university, including syllabus design, lecturing and examining in two languages and Bachelor's thesis supervision. The developmental content is the move from that setting to Earth-observation teaching in English at a Hungarian informatics faculty, and the step up from Bachelor's to doctoral-level supervision. Two concrete measures carry this: co-design and delivery of a full module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture (rather than a single guest lecture), and co-supervision of the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work. Both strengthen the researcher's standing for an independent academic career and feed research results back into teaching at the host.

**Bidirectional knowledge transfer and publications.** The fellowship is a genuine two-way exchange: the host transfers geospatial and data-science competence to the researcher, while the researcher transfers plant physiology, horticultural crop science, plant protection and agronomy, water-stress experimentation, physiological phenotyping, hyperspectral field measurement and the biological interpretation of EO to the host team. This interdisciplinary and inter-sectoral exposure is exactly the new mind-set and approach to R&I work that the call names as its second expected outcome (EO-02). Scientific output is planned around four principal outputs (P1 physiological and hyperspectral early-warning signatures of processing-tomato water stress; P2 hyperspectral-to-Sentinel scaling; P3 temporal and cross-country transferability; P4 research-to-commercial transfer and decision-oriented evaluation of agricultural AI), with at least two high-quality peer-reviewed submissions targeted during or shortly after the fellowship. Networking and public-engagement capacity is developed through one public field demonstration with AgroVIR farmers and one public-facing article per year, with science communication carried as one of the seven transferable-skill strands.

### Specific measures outside academia

**A non-academic placement that supplies the inter-sectoral half of the profile.** The single most decisive employability measure beyond academia is a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR, taken over the final period of the 30-month action (M25 to M30), at the company's site in Hungary. Its added value for the researcher's career is specific and cannot be provided by the academic host: operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation, and direct exposure to commercial agricultural-software requirements. This is the segment of the target profile that makes the researcher employable in precision-agriculture, irrigation-technology and farm-management-information-system (FMIS) companies as well as in academia, satisfying the call's requirement (SR-06) that an optional non-academic placement be an integral, justified and evaluable part of the proposal with explicit added value for the researcher's career development. The placement work content is defined and training-oriented rather than being an engineering favour to the host: operational hardening of the prediction pipeline in a production FMIS environment; the nine-dimension operational assessment producing the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation; the FMIS integration roadmap written from inside the implementing company; and requirements engineering and user testing with commercial growers. The placement is hosted inside the company because the operational assessment, farmer-field access and integration roadmap all depend on the company's own operational environment and customer-facing requirements. On-site supervision during the placement is provided at senior research grade, giving the placement the supervisory seniority its training argument relies on.

**A concrete post-fellowship trajectory.** The action does not end at the fellowship boundary. It produces a research-to-operation delivery path with a named post-MSCA FMIS integration route (the FMIS integration roadmap), so the researcher leaves with a defined onward trajectory in operational agricultural technology rather than an open-ended search. This is the inter-sectoral counterpart to the academic publications track and materially broadens the researcher's options across sectors.

### Expected contribution of the skills development to the future career

Taken together, the measures assemble a distinctive and durable scientific profile: biological understanding, scalable geospatial prediction and operational decision support, combined in one researcher and carried by an agreed and reviewed Career Development Plan (the OC6 career outcome). This combination is deliberately rare, and the project states where it is valued: European research institutes and universities, EU agricultural and environmental research, EO organisations, and precision-agriculture, irrigation-technology and FMIS providers. The academic-track measures (advanced modelling competence, first-author publications, teaching and doctoral co-supervision, Open Science practice) equip the researcher for an independent academic position; the inter-sectoral measures (operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation, commercial requirements engineering, a named FMIS integration route) equip her for a senior applied-research or R&D role in industry. Because the transferable-skill strands (research integrity, Open Science and FAIR practice, generative-AI literacy, grant writing, IP and exploitation, project management, science communication) are sector-agnostic, they raise employability on both tracks simultaneously. The credibility of these claims rests on their being operationalised and reviewed: each is embedded in the Career Development Plan, exercised on a real work package or the placement, reviewed at five points across the action, and — for the plan itself — tracked by a dedicated KPI. In consequence, the action delivers the call's expected outcomes for supported fellows (increased research and transferable skills, EO-01; new inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary mind-sets, EO-02) and contributes to the expected impact of improved researcher employability and career mobility within and beyond academia (EI-01), with the Career Development Plan (D1.3) and the non-academic placement as the two mapped project measures that make that impact concrete.

sub_sections.title: Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities
sub_sections.content:
## 2.2 Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities

### Logic and proportionality of the plan

FIELDWISE is a single-researcher, 30-month European Fellowship hosted at ELTE, with a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR over M25-M30. Its dissemination, exploitation and communication (DEC) measures are therefore sized to what one fellow, supported by the host and three associated partners, can credibly deliver, rather than to a large-consortium outreach machine. Proportionality is made concrete in the effort plan: a dedicated cross-cutting allocation of 3.0 of the fellow's 30 person-months, running the full M1-M30 span, covers management, training and dissemination continuously, so DEC is resourced from the outset rather than deferred to the closing months. The plan keeps the three functions distinct in the MSCA sense — dissemination transfers results to those who can use them scientifically or professionally; exploitation converts results into operational and economic value; and communication raises awareness among the wider public. It also answers, directly, a criticism the draft records against a previous submission: that the economic and technological route to users and the IP strategy were insufficiently substantiated (draft §2.2 ¶233). Each measure below names its user, its route and, where relevant, its IP posture, so the plan is verifiable rather than declarative.

### Dissemination: outputs, target groups and Open Science

Scientific dissemination is built on peer-reviewed, open-access publication of the project's core findings: the physiologically grounded early-warning signatures of processing-tomato water stress; the methodological bridge from high-information proximal hyperspectral observation to scalable Sentinel-based prediction (IMP-SCI); the prospective, uncertainty-aware prediction results; and the temporal and cross-country transferability evidence. Publications are organised around four principal outputs (P1 early-warning signatures; P2 hyperspectral-to-Sentinel scaling; P3 temporal and cross-country transferability; P4 research-to-commercial transfer and decision-oriented evaluation), with at least two high-quality peer-reviewed submissions targeted during or shortly after the fellowship, and submission timing aligned from the mid-fellowship steering point onward with the release of the Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library and the FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card.

Beyond papers, FIELDWISE disseminates reusable research artefacts. The Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library is released as an open output carrying an explicit transferable-or-hyperspectral-only verdict against each candidate feature. The FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card is released with a published model card documenting the engine. The Adaptation protocol states the minimum local-calibration volume needed to move the model to a new agro-environment. The Hungary->Bulgaria transferability report is delivered directly to the international partner, Prof. Vinelina Yankova at MVCRI, reporting both zero-shot and locally calibrated performance. Target groups are addressed by output: agricultural remote-sensing and geoinformatics researchers and crop-stress modelling scientists for the publications and transfer library; Earth-observation and agricultural-AI research groups for the reusable feature-transfer methods; and research organisations adapting the engine to new regions, including MATE and MVCRI, for the engine, model card and adaptation protocol. All outputs follow an Open Science posture — 'as open as possible, as closed as necessary' — with publications in open access, code and model cards released where IP permits, and research data curated to be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable (FAIR) under a data management plan. This satisfies the call's requirement (SR-04) that training foster an Open Science culture, knowledge valorisation and research integrity, and it operationalises expected outcome EO-03 on enhanced networking and communication with peers and the public.

### Exploitation: from validated science to a named operational route

Exploitation is the axis the prior evaluation found thin, and FIELDWISE addresses it with a concrete research-to-operation delivery path (outcome OC5). First, the project advances the DrR research prototype to a scientifically validated DrR web MVP, delivered at M24 — before the placement window — serving stress probability, uncertainty, spatial risk, irrigation priority and temporal evolution (IMP-TECH). Second, that MVP is subjected to an external functional/technical evaluation by the non-academic partner — the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation, covering all nine assessment dimensions — supplying independent evidence on whether the technology meets real agricultural-software requirements, complemented by the Commercial-field transferability assessment and the Field Decision Value report. Third, the FMIS integration roadmap, written from inside the implementing company, names the required interfaces and the concrete post-fellowship steps for embedding the engine in farm-management information systems, giving the action a defined onward exploitation route rather than an open-ended aspiration.

The exploitation audience is precise: precision-agriculture companies, irrigation-technology providers and farm-management-information-system (FMIS) providers, alongside the academic and EO organisations that reuse the methods. AgroVIR's own position makes the route credible — the company runs an FMIS in production use across more than 745,000 hectares in eight countries, including Hungary and Bulgaria, the two countries FIELDWISE works in — although this commercial footprint is an operator-declared characterisation to be confirmed with the partner. The Adaptation protocol extends exploitation geographically, letting other European regions re-calibrate the models at a stated minimum cost (IMP-EU). These measures are the mapped mechanisms behind expected impacts EI-02 (strengthened inter-sectoral and international collaboration) and EI-05 (increased R&I capacity, output and knowledge transfer).

### Communication activities

Public communication is delivered through two proportionate, recurring actions: one public field demonstration of the decision-support tool with AgroVIR growers, held during the placement, which shows in-field how the tool supports irrigation timing and stress detection and gathers grower feedback; and one public-facing article per year, written in accessible language for the interested public and the regional and agricultural-sector press. The target audiences are deliberately non-academic — processing-tomato growers and farm operators in the AgroVIR network, and the general public — and the objective is to broaden public engagement with the research and public understanding of transferable agricultural AI for water-efficient farming. These are the mapped measures for expected impact EI-03 and they reinforce expected outcome EO-03. They are recorded honestly as recurring activities carried by the cross-cutting dissemination allocation, since no separate work-package deliverable is claimed to carry them; a formal dissemination deliverable could be added, but inventing one here is avoided.

### Intellectual-property strategy and protection measures

The default IP posture is open: the predictive engine is released with a published model card, and the transfer library and adaptation protocol are published as reusable outputs, so value is captured primarily through open release and non-academic uptake rather than formal protection. No patent or other formal protection is presently claimed; any protectable outcome identified during the AgroVIR evaluation and the FMIS-roadmap work would be assessed jointly by the host and the partner before any disclosure, preserving the option to protect where warranted. Background IP is handled explicitly. The DrR components brought by the fellow are recorded as her background IP, and because the six-month placement involves work touching that prototype inside a commercial partner, ownership of placement results is set to follow the grant-agreement default, vesting in ELTE as the beneficiary acting through the fellow, with a written placement agreement between the fellow, ELTE and AgroVIR — concluded before the placement begins — confirming this allocation and the access terms to the DrR background IP. This ownership arrangement rests on an operator-adopted position pending that agreement, and is presented as a foreseen measure rather than a settled fact. Taken together, the naming of users, of the operational route and of the background-IP allocation is what substantiates the economic/technological route to users and the IP strategy that the previous submission was found to leave insufficiently substantiated (draft §2.2 ¶233).

### Sustainability, and mapping to the call's expected impacts

Results persist beyond the fellowship through durable, project-grounded channels: the released FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card and the FMIS integration roadmap provide a maintainable, integrable software asset and a validated post-fellowship uptake path; the open Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library and the Adaptation protocol let other European regions reuse and re-calibrate the methods; integration of results into ELTE teaching — co-design and delivery of a full module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture, and co-supervision of the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work — carries the knowledge into education (EI-06); and the agreed and reviewed Career Development Plan sustains the fellow's own capacity to continue the line of work (EI-01). Each DEC measure is tied to a project deliverable and, where applicable, to a KPI — the per-feature transferability verdicts recorded in the transfer library, the published model card for the released engine, the nine-dimension coverage of the AgroVIR evaluation, and the interfaces and post-fellowship steps named in the FMIS roadmap — so the plan can be verified both during and after the action. In sum, the measures deliver the covered expected impacts EI-02 and EI-05 through mapped deliverables, deliver EI-03 through recurring public-engagement activities, contribute to EI-06 through the integration of results into teaching, and reinforce EI-01 through the exploitation route and the Career Development Plan, proportionately to a single-researcher action.

sub_sections.title: The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts
sub_sections.content:
## 2.3 The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts

### How FIELDWISE makes a difference beyond its immediate scope

FIELDWISE is a single-researcher, 30-month European Fellowship whose experimental object is deliberately narrow — physiologically grounded water-stress prediction in processing tomato, developed at ELTE and tested from Hungary to Bulgaria and from research fields to commercial farming. Its contribution to impact, however, is designed to generalise well beyond that object. The action defines five distinct impact channels — scientific (IMP-SCI), environmental (IMP-ENV), agricultural and food-production (IMP-AGRI), technological (IMP-TECH) and European (IMP-EU) — and each is constructed so that the difference it makes outlasts the fellowship and detaches from the specific crop, region and sensor archive on which it was first demonstrated. The magnitude of that difference is expressed, throughout this section, through what the project actually controls and delivers: reusable outputs, an externally evaluated operational route, and eleven KPIs each tracing to a named deliverable. Where a credible macro-scale figure exists it is stated; where one would be speculative, the project explicitly refuses to assert it in advance and commits instead to quantifying it from project evidence — a discipline that is itself a mark of the estimate's credibility rather than a gap in it.

### Scientific impact: a transferability-based evaluation paradigm and a portable sensor-domain bridge (IMP-SCI)

The project's scientific contribution has two components, and both are consequential beyond the immediate result. First, FIELDWISE provides a framework for agricultural AI evaluated according to temporal, geographic and operational transferability rather than only retrospective accuracy. This is a methodological reorientation, not a single dataset: it replaces the field's dominant habit of scoring models on in-distribution R², RMSE or classification accuracy with an evaluation that asks whether a model still performs on an unseen season, in a second country, and under commercial-field heterogeneity — and, ultimately, whether it is useful for an irrigation decision at all. Because the paradigm is about how models are judged rather than about tomato specifically, its importance extends to any crop, sensor and region where agricultural intelligence must move from the field in which it was trained to the field in which it must operate. Second, the action establishes a methodological bridge between high-information proximal hyperspectral observations and scalable Sentinel-based prediction — a bridge that answers a general question (which locally discovered spectral signatures survive translation to freely available satellite resolution) that recurs across precision-agriculture applications far beyond this project.

The magnitude of this scientific contribution is made verifiable through outputs the project controls. The Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library records, for every candidate hyperspectral feature, an explicit transferable-or-hyperspectral-only verdict, so the sensor-domain bridge is delivered as an auditable, reusable artefact rather than an assertion. The FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card is released with a published model card documenting the engine, making the model interrogable and reusable by other groups. The prospective forecasting capability is evaluated at multiple actionable horizons (t+1, t+3 and t+5) with reported calibration and prediction-interval coverage, and field-level usefulness is measured by computing Field Decision Value for at least two competing models with lead time, false-action rate and missed-stress rate reported — directly instantiating, and testing, the hypothesis that the most retrospectively accurate model is not necessarily the most useful one. These findings are disseminated by peer-reviewed open-access publication, with at least two high-quality submissions targeted during or shortly after the fellowship, so the paradigm and the bridge enter the scientific record and contribute to the enriched, cross-boundary European R&I culture the call sets as a systemic scientific impact (EI-02).

### Economic and technological impact: a concrete, externally validated route from research to operational use (IMP-TECH)

FIELDWISE advances the work from a desktop research prototype to a scientifically validated web MVP — the DrR web MVP, delivered at M24, before the placement window — and then subjects that MVP to external functional and technical evaluation by the non-academic partner. This is the axis on which the project's economic and technological magnitude is most concrete, because the route to users is named rather than aspirational. The AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation supplies independent evidence, across all nine assessment dimensions, on whether the resulting technology meets the requirements of real agricultural software, and the FMIS integration roadmap — written from inside the implementing company — names the required interfaces and the concrete post-fellowship steps for embedding the engine in farm-management information systems. Together these constitute a research-to-operation delivery path (outcome OC5): an externally evaluated MVP plus a named post-MSCA integration route, which is precisely the kind of onward exploitation trajectory that converts a fellowship result into economic value beyond the action.

The importance of this route is amplified by the nature of the uptake channel. The named exploitation partner operates a farm-management information system in production use across more than 745,000 hectares in eight countries, including Hungary and Bulgaria — the two countries in which FIELDWISE works — which indicates a realistic scale at which a validated engine could be adopted rather than shelved; this commercial footprint is an operator-declared characterisation to be confirmed with the partner, and it is presented as such rather than as an established fact. The economic relevance is grounded in the application itself: processing tomato is a high-value horticultural test case in which improved irrigation timing bears directly on productivity, fruit quality, water-use efficiency and economic return, so even modest gains in decision quality translate into agronomic and economic value in a crop system where the margin for mistiming is narrow. At the systemic level, this strengthens the R&I capacity, output and knowledge-transfer standing of the participating organisations that the call identifies as an economic impact (EI-05), through reusable, uptake-ready outputs rather than through claims.

### Societal and environmental impact: better irrigation decisions against a quantified European water problem (IMP-ENV, IMP-AGRI)

The societal significance of the contribution is anchored in a quantified statement of the problem it addresses. Approximately 30% of EU territory is affected by seasonal water scarcity in an average year, and water scarcity already translates into agricultural yield losses and higher water costs, while irrigation demand is expected to increase under climate change. Against this backdrop, FIELDWISE contributes to the EU-level opportunity for water savings in irrigated agriculture by improving the timing and spatial prioritisation of irrigation decisions — the two levers a physiologically grounded, uncertainty-aware, spatially explicit forecast is positioned to move. This is the channel through which the project's results make a societal difference beyond their immediate scope: an irrigation-timing capability validated on processing tomato and released with a stated adaptation cost is reusable against the same water-scarcity pressure in other high-value crops and regions.

Crucially, the project bounds this claim honestly. It does not assert in advance that it will achieve a particular percentage reduction in water use; the environmental impact will be quantified from project evidence rather than promised as a headline figure. This restraint is deliberate and is the credible form of the estimate: the magnitude is expressed through what the project can demonstrate — earlier, calibrated warnings; measured field-level decision value; spatial prioritisation of where irrigation matters most — rather than through an unfounded macro-number that an evaluator would rightly discount. Public understanding of transferable agricultural AI for water-efficient farming is broadened through the recurring public-engagement activities set out in the dissemination and communication plan (contributing to EI-03), so the societal benefit reaches growers and the wider public and not only the scientific audience.

### European impact: transferability as a continent-scale question, with a stated cost of reuse (IMP-EU)

The project's European dimension is more than a two-country test; it is a direct investigation of a question that limits the value of locally developed agricultural intelligence across Europe. The MATE and MVCRI architecture investigates whether agricultural AI developed in one European environment can be transferred to another, and FIELDWISE thereby contributes to the wider European question of how locally developed agricultural intelligence can become reliably transferable rather than remaining confined to the field in which it was trained. The magnitude of this contribution is made tangible and, importantly, quantifiable in the dimension that matters for reuse: the Adaptation protocol states the minimum local-calibration volume needed to move the model to a new agro-environment, and the Hungary->Bulgaria transferability report reports both zero-shot and locally calibrated performance and is delivered to Prof. Vinelina Yankova at MVCRI. Stating the adaptation cost converts an abstract transferability claim into an operational one — a research group or agri-technology provider in another European region can read, in advance, how much local data it would take to re-calibrate the models — and that is what lets the contribution scale beyond the specific Hungary-to-Bulgaria corridor. Together with the openly released transfer library, the documented predictive engine and the adaptation protocol, this sustains a cross-European knowledge-transfer contribution (EI-05) whose reach is limited by adoption effort rather than by the models being locked to their training site.

### Magnitude and importance, taken together

The importance of FIELDWISE's contribution rests on the fact that it addresses a systemic weakness the field has largely tolerated — models optimised for retrospective accuracy that fail on unseen seasons, in new countries, or under commercial conditions — and replaces it with an evaluation paradigm, a portable sensor-domain method, a stated cost of geographic reuse, and an externally evaluated operational route. Its magnitude is presented in the register an evaluator can check: a quantified statement of the European water problem it serves; deliverable-anchored KPIs that bound each claim (per-feature transferability verdicts, a published model card, calibrated multi-horizon forecasts, Field Decision Value across competing models, a nine-dimension external evaluation, a named FMIS integration route, a stated minimum calibration volume); and a deliberate refusal to attach a speculative water-saving percentage to results that have not yet been produced. This combination — ambition that reaches beyond processing tomato, coupled with estimates disciplined to what the action controls — is what makes the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts both material and credible, proportionately to a single-researcher fellowship.

FIELDWISE provides a framework for agricultural AI evaluated by temporal, geographic and operational transferability rather than only retrospective accuracy, and establishes a methodological bridge from proximal hyperspectral observation to scalable Sentinel-based prediction, with impact beyond the specific crop/region.

The project contributes to the EU-level opportunity for water savings by improving irrigation timing and spatial prioritisation, and explicitly does not claim a particular percentage reduction in advance, committing to quantify impact from project evidence.

Water scarcity already causes agricultural yield losses and higher water costs and irrigation demand is expected to rise; processing tomato is a high-value horticultural test case where improved timing has substantial agronomic and economic relevance.
FIELDWISE advances a desktop research prototype to a scientifically validated web MVP that is externally evaluated by AgroVIR for fitness against real agricultural-software requirements.

The MATE-MVCRI architecture investigates whether agricultural AI developed in one European environment transfers to another, contributing to the wider European question of making locally developed agricultural intelligence reliably transferable.

Approximately 30% of EU territory is affected by seasonal water scarcity in an average year, with water scarcity already translating into yield losses and higher water costs and irrigation demand expected to increase under climate change.
